leading_positions.synthesis: Six of eight round-1 files prefer a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Shared: Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrations, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier; agreement across independent laboratories at about 1e-18; and the view that a third name or a second part should not be added. Not shared: how much weight the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize should carry against it, and how tightly the citation must be drawn. Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce cite the breadth of opening support, and Lindroth and Olsson say they checked the case on its own merits; Danielsson explicitly conditions his support on evidence of competitive physics bounds, and Olsson keeps B056 and B054 as alternatives and says her own first choice B056 should be discounted for disciplinary bias. The citation wordings differ (invention and realisation, 10^-18 regime, new tests of fundamental physics, development to unprecedented accuracy).

Eriksson alone prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, with a two-laureate configuration (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) rather than the three-name ballot credit including Bistritzer, and a citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the experimental discovery of the correlated and superconducting phases. Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson accept the two-name shape as cleaner if the committee goes this way, while Lindroth, Johansson, Danielsson and Pearce raise the unresolved pairing mechanism and field age as reasons to wait. Eriksson lists B007 and B042 as alternatives and says he would not oppose B042 if the AMO members find its attribution clean.

Mehlig alone prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a theory-plus-experiment trio, arguing the Z2 classification is distinct from the 2016 topology prize and has been stable and confirmed in many materials. He names the omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu (and, for 3D, Moore and Hasan) as the real weak point of his own choice and gives B042 as his fallback. B007 appears as an alternative for Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth.

areas_of_agreement: Every member who discusses optical lattice clocks (all eight files mention it) treats the physics as sound and independently reproduced across national laboratories; Mehlig, who prefers B007, calls the clocks an excellent candidate and his fallback, and Eriksson lists B042 as an alternative.

Six of eight members explicitly prefer B042 with Katori and Ye as the only two laureates; Lindroth and Johansson say they would not add a third name, and Kroll and Pearce say they would not join it to a second part or favour splitting the prize.

Cavity optomechanics (B023) is not put forward by any member in a preferred configuration; Pearce and Kroll say they would not put it in a final configuration, and Johansson says he would recuse himself from any configuration containing it.

Several members (Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Pearce) say a very large collaboration makes a two- or three-name credit hard to defend for B026 and B029, and Kroll and Lindroth say the B010 credit of four names exceeds the three-laureate limit.

The citation for any clock prize should be anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its demonstration, not on clocks or combs in general (stated by Lindroth, Johansson, Olsson and Pearce).
scientific_disputes: Whether optical lattice clocks are a discovery about nature or primarily a measurement achievement: Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson note that fundamental-physics results (gravity, constants, dark matter) so far are null results or prospective, while Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Olsson cite millimetre-scale redshift measurements and existing bounds as already physics.

Whether a new class of quantum matter (Mehlig on B007; Eriksson on B054) should weigh more heavily than a further gain in precision, as Mehlig argues, or whether a new measurement regime that opens many experiments deserves equal weight, as Pearce, Kroll and Olsson argue.

For B054, whether the flat-band prediction, correlated insulators and superconducting domes are stable and reproduced (Eriksson) even though the pairing mechanism is unresolved (Lindroth, Johansson, Danielsson, Pearce), and how much twist-angle disorder and sample variability limit the claim that the phases are intrinsic.

For B029, whether the diffuse-flux detection is solid but source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still partial and the origin of most of the flux unresolved (Danielsson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce).

Whether the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize make a lattice-clock prize a successor step (Lindroth, Johansson, Kroll, Olsson, Pearce, Mehlig all flag it) or a distinct physical idea; Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll argue the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from single-ion quantum logic, while Pearce notes critics may link Ye's comb-linked comparisons to Hall and Hansch.
attribution_disputes: B042: Whether Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto, Ludlow, the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups and the Al+ ion-clock tradition have claims a two-name credit cannot absorb; Danielsson and Lindroth ask for primary-literature evidence for any third name, while Johansson and Pearce ask that the reasons for excluding them be recorded.

B042: Whether Ye's claim rests on distinct inventions (many-body and comb-linked clock physics) or mainly on accuracy records, which Olsson warns is a later and better experiment; Kroll and Olsson want the citation to say explicitly why Katori and Ye are named.

B007: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested, and Fu, Moore, Hasan and others are central to 3D topological insulators; Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce raise this, and Mehlig accepts it as the real weak point of B007.

B054: Whether two laureates (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero) or three including Bistritzer is fairer, and how to treat experimental first authors Cao and Fatemi and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto (Eriksson, Olsson, Danielsson).

B029 and B026: Halzen is clear but Spiering's role is described as programme leadership across Baikal and IceCube (Danielsson, Olsson, Pearce), AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors are not credited, and three leaders from ATLAS and CMS collaborations of thousands cannot represent the decisive ideas (Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Pearce).
maturity_disputes: B054: Eriksson says reproduction by many independent groups is fast and broad; Danielsson, Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce say the field is under ten years old, the pairing mechanism is open and the interpretation is still moving. Eriksson accepts that waiting is a possibility and asks Pearce whether a timing argument undervalues speed of confirmation.

B042: Kroll treats the pending redefinition of the second as a near-term reason for timeliness, Danielsson calls it a metrological milestone and not a physical discovery, and Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig note that geodesy, the redefinition and impact beyond metrology are still pending or prospective.

B029: Pearce, Olsson and Lindroth place IceCube behind the clocks on source identification and attribution, with Olsson suggesting keeping it under review for a year, while Danielsson would support a neutrino-led configuration if the expert reports are strong.
B010: Kroll notes the 2D Fermi-Hubbard payoff is still developing and the 2001 BEC prize covers part of the cooling toolbox.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson directs WACQT and works at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting quantum circuits and has a personal collaboration touching B023 (Cleland); he would recuse from any configuration including B023. No connection to Katori or Ye.

Kroll spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during his PhD, Jun Ye is associated with Hall's JILA environment, and Kroll is on the WACQT executive management team (overlapping institutionally with Chalmers, Johansson's home); no collaboration with Ye or Katori and he sees no recusal requirement.

Olsson is a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and Katori is at the University of Tokyo (collegial, not collaborative); she is also invested in B056 as a microscopist and a Chalmers colleague of Johansson.
Lindroth collaborates closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and her Lund group, outside the shortlist, and says she would recuse herself if a closer tie to a candidate emerges.

Pearce (chair) is in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, not in IceCube or the EHT, with professional familiarity with the B029 and B047 communities; he would flag a possible recusal question if either became the leading proposal.

Danielsson notes B047 (black hole shadow) lies close to his research interests but does not see this as a reason for recusal; Johansson notes he is an interested theorist in a field neighbouring AMO and may overrate clean controllable quantum systems; Mehlig shares the Gothenburg environment with Johansson and Olsson (institutional, not a recusal issue).
questions_for_round2: For B042, what wording of a Katori-Ye citation distinguishes the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and does it need to name why Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Derevianko, PTB, NIST and SYRTE are not credited?

Is there primary-literature evidence that a third named contributor to the lattice-clock concept has a real claim, and if so who, or is the two-name credit defensible as stated by Danielsson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson?

Have lattice-clock comparisons produced competitive bounds on varying constants, ultralight dark matter or gravity, or is the fundamental-physics payoff still prospective (Danielsson's condition), and how should that weigh in a discovery-focused prize?

Do Eriksson and Mehlig accept B042 as the committee's leading proposal, and if not, what specific evidence on B054 (pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder, treatment of Cao and Fatemi) or on B007 (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, and the size of the overlap with 2016) would change the preference?
Is the B007 attribution problem resolvable within three names, and how large is the overlap between the Z2 classification and the 2016 topology prize, as Olsson, Pearce and Johansson ask Mehlig?

Should any other proposal (B029, B010, B026, B056) be kept as a live alternative to B042, and what attribution evidence for IceCube (Spiering's role, AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND) or the Higgs observation (credit among ATLAS and CMS) would be needed to do so?

Do the disclosed connections of Kroll (Hall laboratory, JILA, WACQT), Olsson (University of Tokyo) and Lindroth (Lund group) need any committee handling before a vote on B042, and does the committee want any guidance on this?
summary.chair_observation: The round-1 record is concentrated: six of eight files prefer B042 with Katori and Ye, one prefers B054 with two laureates and one prefers B007. The B042 support is shared in outcome but rests on different reasons and a few members attach conditions. The minority positions are not rejected on the science; they are questioned mainly on maturity (B054) and attribution and overlap with 2016 (B007). Because the committee's own opening rankings partly drove the movement towards B042, round 2 should test the clock case on its own evidence, especially novelty against 2005 and 2012, the two-name credit, and the fundamental-physics payoff.
